title: Chemical Bonding II (Geometry) - Chemistry - VSEPR Theory
subject: Chemistry

questions.q: According to VSEPR theory, what is the primary factor that determines the arrangement of electron pairs around a central atom?
options: Maximizing the attraction between the nucleus and electrons.
Minimizing the electrostatic repulsion between valence electron pairs.
Maximizing the number of bonds formed.
questions.explain: The VSEPR model assumes that electron pairs in the valence shell of a central atom will adopt an arrangement that minimizes repulsions between these electron pairs by maximizing the distance between them.[[1](https://www.google.com/url?sa=E&q=https%3A%2F%2Fchem.libretexts.org%2FBookshelves%2FGeneral_Chemistry%2FMap%253A_Chemistry_-_The_Central_Science_(Brown_et_al.)%2F11%253A_Liquids_and_Intermolecular_Forces%2F11.02%253A_Intermolecular_Forces)][[2](https://www.google.com/url?sa=E&q=https%3A%2F%2Fopenstax.org%2Fbooks%2Fchemistry-2e%2Fpages%2F7-6-molecular-structure-and-polarity)] [Source: OpenStax](https://openstax.org/books/chemistry-2e/pages/7-6-molecular-structure-and-polarity)
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following correctly lists the order of electron-pair repulsions from greatest to least?
options: bonding pair-bonding pair > lone pair-bonding pair > lone pair-lone pair
lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bonding pair > bonding pair-bonding pair
lone pair-bonding pair > bonding pair-bonding pair > lone pair-lone pair
bonding pair-bonding pair > lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bonding pair
questions.explain: Lone pairs occupy more space than bonding pairs, leading to stronger repulsions.[[1](https://www.google.com/url?sa=E&q=https%3A%2F%2Fchem.libretexts.org%2FBookshelves%2FGeneral_Chemistry%2FMap%253A_Chemistry_-_The_Central_Science_(Brown_et_al.)%2F11%253A_Liquids_and_Intermolecular_Forces%2F11.02%253A_Intermolecular_Forces)][[2](https://www.google.com/url?sa=E&q=https%3A%2F%2Fopenstax.org%2Fbooks%2Fchemistry-2e%2Fpages%2F7-6-molecular-structure-and-polarity)] The order is: lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bonding pair > bonding pair-bonding pair. [Source: OpenStax](https://openstax.org/books/chemistry-2e/pages/7-6-molecular-structure-and-polarity)
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: In the VSEPR model, how is a double or triple bond treated when counting regions of electron density?
options: A double bond counts as 2 regions; a triple bond counts as 3 regions.
Multiple bonds are not counted as regions of electron density.
A single, double, or triple bond each counts as exactly one region of electron density.

A double bond counts as 1 region, but a triple bond counts as 2 regions.[[1](https://www.google.com/url?sa=E&q=https%3A%2F%2Fchem.libretexts.org%2FBookshelves%2FGeneral_Chemistry%2FMap%253A_Chemistry_-_The_Central_Science_(Brown_et_al.)%2F11%253A_Liquids_and_Intermolecular_Forces%2F11.02%253A_Intermolecular_Forces)]
questions.explain: We count the number of regions of electron density (lone pairs and bonds) around the central atom.[[1](https://www.google.com/url?sa=E&q=https%3A%2F%2Fchem.libretexts.org%2FBookshelves%2FGeneral_Chemistry%2FMap%253A_Chemistry_-_The_Central_Science_(Brown_et_al.)%2F11%253A_Liquids_and_Intermolecular_Forces%2F11.02%253A_Intermolecular_Forces)][[2](https://www.google.com/url?sa=E&q=https%3A%2F%2Fopenstax.org%2Fbooks%2Fchemistry-2e%2Fpages%2F7-6-molecular-structure-and-polarity)][[3](https://www.google.com/url?sa=E&q=https%3A%2F%2Fopenstax.org%2Fbooks%2Fchemistry-2e%2Fpages%2F8-2-hybrid-atomic-orbitals)] A single, double, or triple bond counts as one region of electron density.[[1](https://www.google.com/url?sa=E&q=https%3A%2F%2Fchem.libretexts.org%2FBookshelves%2FGeneral_Chemistry%2FMap%253A_Chemistry_-_The_Central_Science_(Brown_et_al.)%2F11%253A_Liquids_and_Intermolecular_Forces%2F11.02%253A_Intermolecular_Forces)][[2](https://www.google.com/url?sa=E&q=https%3A%2F%2Fopenstax.org%2Fbooks%2Fchemistry-2e%2Fpages%2F7-6-molecular-structure-and-polarity)][[4](https://www.google.com/url?sa=E&q=https%3A%2F%2Fopenstax.org%2Fbooks%2Fchemistry-2e%2Fpages%2F8-4-molecular-orbital-theory)] [Source: OpenStax](https://openstax.org/books/chemistry-2e/pages/7-6-molecular-structure-and-polarity)

questions.q: Why are the bond angles in ammonia ($NH_3$) and water ($H_2O$) slightly less than the ideal tetrahedral angle of $109.5^\circ$?
options: The atoms are too large to fit the ideal angle.
Lone pairs occupy a larger region of space than bonding pairs, compressing the bond angles.
The bonds in these molecules are ionic rather than covalent.
The central atoms are $sp^2$ hybridized rather than $sp^3$.
questions.explain: The bond angles are slightly smaller than 109.5° because the lone pair-bonding pair repulsion is greater than the bonding pair-bonding pair repulsion, taking up more space.[[1](https://www.google.com/url?sa=E&q=https%3A%2F%2Fchem.libretexts.org%2FBookshelves%2FGeneral_Chemistry%2FMap%253A_Chemistry_-_The_Central_Science_(Brown_et_al.)%2F11%253A_Liquids_and_Intermolecular_Forces%2F11.02%253A_Intermolecular_Forces)][[2](https://www.google.com/url?sa=E&q=https%3A%2F%2Fopenstax.org%2Fbooks%2Fchemistry-2e%2Fpages%2F7-6-molecular-structure-and-polarity)][[3](https://www.google.com/url?sa=E&q=https%3A%2F%2Fopenstax.org%2Fbooks%2Fchemistry-2e%2Fpages%2F8-2-hybrid-atomic-orbitals)][[4](https://www.google.com/url?sa=E&q=https%3A%2F%2Fopenstax.org%2Fbooks%2Fchemistry-2e%2Fpages%2F8-4-molecular-orbital-theory)][[5](https://www.google.com/url?sa=E&q=https%3A%2F%2Fchem.libretexts.org%2FBookshelves%2FGeneral_Chemistry%2FMap%253A_General_Chemistry_(Petrucci_et_al.)%2F10%253A_Chemical_Bonding_II_-_Valence_Bond_and_Molecular_Orbital_Theory%2F10.02%253A_VSEPR_Theory_and_Molecular_Shapes)] [Source: OpenStax](https://openstax.org/books/chemistry-2e/pages/7-6-molecular-structure-and-polarity)
